prompt: Which command creates the default route shown?
options: ip default-gateway 10.0.12.2
explanation: A default route has destination 0.0.0.0 and mask 0.0.0.0, with the next hop 10.0.12.2.

whyWrong.0: ip default-gateway is for a non-routing device and does not create a static route.
whyWrong.1: A /32 mask matches one address, not all.
whyWrong.2: That names the transit subnet as the destination.

prompt: A floating static route loses to a healthy primary. Which command shows the configured backup line?
options: show ip route static
show interfaces
show running-config
show ip arp
explanation: show running-config lists every configured static route, including one not installed in the routing table.

whyWrong.0: show ip route static lists installed routes only, so it omits the floating route.
whyWrong.1: Interface output does not list static routes.
whyWrong.3: ARP shows address resolution, not routes.

prompt: A static route to 10.9.0.0/16 names exit interface Gi0/1 and next hop 10.0.13.2. What does it do?
options: It requires ARP resolution for each host in the remote /16.
It names 10.0.13.2 as the remote destination prefix.
It forwards the /16 through Gi0/1 without using an IP next hop.
It directs the remote /16 to 10.0.13.2 through Gi0/1.
explanation: The destination and mask define 10.9.0.0/16, and the interface and next hop give the exit. Traffic goes to 10.0.13.2 out Gi0/1.

whyWrong.0: The frame goes to the next hop's MAC, not to each remote host.
whyWrong.1: 10.9.0.0/16 is the destination, and 10.0.13.2 is the next router.
whyWrong.2: The route names an IP next hop as well as the interface.

prompt: A traceroute from PC-A lists R1, R2 and PC-B. What does it show?
options: The reverse data path must use exactly the same interfaces.
The trace reached PC-B and received its responses.
No route in the network can change.
Every application on PC-B is healthy.
explanation: A completed trace shows the probes reached PC-B and its replies came back at that time. It does not prove the reply path is the same or that applications work.

whyWrong.0: Replies can use a different path.
whyWrong.2: Routes can change later.
whyWrong.3: Applications need their own tests.

prompt: How does a static route learn that a remote application has failed?
options: It does not provide an application health check by itself
It receives periodic updates from the static next hop
It polls that application whenever the metric is zero
It detects the failure from its configured prefix length
explanation: A static route is only forwarding information. It cannot monitor an application unless you add tracking.

whyWrong.1: Static routes do not receive updates.
whyWrong.2: A static route does not poll applications.
whyWrong.3: A prefix length describes destinations, not health.

prompt: Only server 10.20.30.40 must use neighbor 172.16.1.2. Which route leaves the rest of 10.20.30.0/24 alone?
explanation: A host route with mask 255.255.255.255 matches only 10.20.30.40.

whyWrong.1: The /24 covers the whole subnet.
whyWrong.2: The default covers every destination.
whyWrong.3: IOS rejects a host address with a /24 mask.

prompt: Gi0/0 is Ethernet and the remote-LAN route names only the interface. What results?
options: R1 treats covered destinations as on-link and may ARP for each destination.
R1 automatically discovers the correct IP next hop using CDP.
The route is a connected interface route with code C.
R1 uses 192.168.20.0 as the next router address.
explanation: Without a next hop, R1 treats the destinations as on-link and may ARP for each one. Use a next hop for a remote LAN.

whyWrong.1: CDP does not supply a next hop.
whyWrong.2: The route is still static (S), not connected.
whyWrong.3: The prefix is the destination, not a router.

prompt: OSPF has a route to 10.5.0.0/16 at AD 110. Which two statements describe a static backup for the same prefix? (Choose two.)
options: Distance 5 makes the route less preferred than OSPF.
Distance 255 is the safest usable standby value.
The backup's next hop must still be usable when it is needed.
A usable backup can have distance 120.
explanation: A backup must have a higher AD than OSPF, such as 120, and a usable next hop when the OSPF route disappears.

whyWrong.0: AD 5 is lower than 110, so the static would be preferred.
whyWrong.1: AD 255 is never installed.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
Configured:
ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.12.2
Gi0/0: administratively down/down
No covering route to 10.0.12.2 in the installed table.

prompt: The only path to 10.0.12.2 was the connected subnet on Gi0/0, which is now down. Why is the next-hop-only route missing?
options: The remote network must use the transit link's /30 mask.
IOS cannot resolve the configured next hop.
A static route never installs until its destination answers a ping.
Static routes require a routing-protocol neighbor.
explanation: A next-hop-only static route needs a route that resolves the next hop. That route went down with Gi0/0, so IOS removes the static.

whyWrong.0: The destination mask is independent of the transit link.
whyWrong.2: A static route does not wait for a ping to answer.
whyWrong.3: Static routes need no routing protocol neighbor.

prompt: R1 and R2 have defaults pointing at each other and no route to 203.0.113.77. What happens to a packet for that address?
options: The lowest next-hop address breaks the forwarding loop.
It can loop between the routers until its TTL expires.
The router with the lowest static AD becomes the final destination.
The default itself creates an Internet path.
explanation: Each router sends the packet back to the other by its default. TTL drops at each hop and the packet is discarded when it reaches 0.

whyWrong.0: Next-hop address values do not break loops.
whyWrong.2: AD does not make a router the destination.
whyWrong.3: A default route does not create Internet access.

prompt: Both routes shown are installed. Which next hop handles 10.1.0.77?
options: 10.0.13.2, because /24 is the longer match
10.0.12.2, because distance 1 is lower
Neither, because a /32 is required
Both, because every overlapping route load-shares
explanation: 10.1.0.77 matches both prefixes, and the /24 is longer. Longest match decides, not AD.

whyWrong.1: AD is not compared across different prefixes.
whyWrong.2: A network route covers all its addresses.
whyWrong.3: Different prefixes are not equal-cost paths.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
R1: LAN 192.168.10.1/24, transit 10.0.12.1/30
R2: LAN 192.168.20.1/24, transit 10.0.12.2/30
R1 ordinary ping to PC-B succeeds; PC-A ping fails.

prompt: Interfaces and the outbound route are verified, but R2 has no route to 192.168.10.0/24. Which command on R2 fixes the return path?
options: ip default-gateway 192.168.10.1
explanation: R2 needs a route to the PC-A subnet through R1's adjacent address, 10.0.12.1.

whyWrong.0: ip default-gateway does not create a route.
whyWrong.1: R2 already has the PC-B LAN connected, and it is PC-A's LAN that is missing.
whyWrong.2: 10.0.12.2 is R2's own address.

prompt: R1 pings remote PC-B. Which source address tests the return route to R1's LAN 192.168.10.0/24?
options: 10.0.12.2, R2's transit address
192.168.20.12, PC-B's address
192.168.10.1, R1's LAN interface address
10.0.12.1, R1's transit address
explanation: A reply to 192.168.10.1 needs a route to 192.168.10.0/24. Choose that source in an extended ping.

whyWrong.0: R1 cannot use R2's address as its source.
whyWrong.1: PC-B is the destination, not the source.
whyWrong.3: A transit source tests a different prefix.

prompt: R1's primary interface connects to a switch and stays up. A remote router beyond it fails and no tracking is set. What about the backup?
options: Raising the backup distance enables remote-failure detection.
The primary may remain installed despite the remote failure.
Static routes exchange updates and will learn the failure.
The backup installs automatically whenever a remote ping fails.
explanation: Static routing has no end-to-end check. The primary stays installed while the local interface is up, even if the far side fails.

whyWrong.0: AD changes preference, not detection.
whyWrong.2: Static routes exchange no updates.
whyWrong.3: A failed ping does not withdraw the route without tracking.

prompt: The remote LAN is 198.51.100.64/26 and peer 10.0.12.2 is reachable. Which command names that network?
explanation: The /26 mask is 255.255.255.192, and the network address is 198.51.100.64, covering .64 to .127.

whyWrong.0: A /24 mask does not describe a /26.
whyWrong.1: That /26 starts at .0, not .64.
whyWrong.3: 198.51.100.65 has host bits set for this network.

prompt: Which command removes the shown backup and keeps the primary?
explanation: To remove a static route, repeat its prefix, mask, exit interface, next hop and distance with no in front.

whyWrong.0: That is a host route, not the shown /24 backup.
whyWrong.1: That is the primary route.
whyWrong.3: That is a different next-hop-only form.

prompt: R1 reaches the remote LAN through the adjacent R2 interface. Which next hop goes in R1's route?
options: 192.168.20.1, because it is the remote default gateway
192.168.10.11, because it is the requesting client
10.0.12.1, because it is R1’s sending interface
10.0.12.2, because it is R2 on the selected transit
explanation: The next hop is the address of the adjacent router on the transit link, which is R2's 10.0.12.2.

whyWrong.0: That is R2's LAN address, not the adjacent transit peer.
whyWrong.1: That is the source client.
whyWrong.2: That is R1's own address.

exhibit.title: Both configured candidates lose eligibility
exhibit.text:
R1 configured:
ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 Gi0/0 10.0.12.2
ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.13.2 5
Gi0/0 is down. The only route to 10.0.13.2 is also withdrawn.
No other route or default resolves either next hop.

prompt: The primary route is withdrawn. What happens?
options: The configured backup installs because its distance exceeds 1
The router creates a new next-hop route from the remote prefix
No route to the remote /24 can install from these candidates
Both statics remain installed because their configuration remains
explanation: The primary lost its interface, and the next-hop-only backup has no route to resolve its next hop. No route to the remote /24 can be installed.

whyWrong.0: A higher AD does not help without a resolvable next hop.
whyWrong.1: The router does not create new routes.
whyWrong.3: Configuration alone does not install a route.

exhibit.title: Failover with no reverse route
exhibit.text:
PC-A 192.168.10.11/24 → PC-B 192.168.20.12/24; both gateways correct.
After direct Gi0/0 link failure:
R1 installed S 192.168.20.0/24 [5/0] via 10.0.13.2 Gi0/1.
R2 Gi0/1 and both LANs are up; request delivery is observed.
R2 has no route or default for 192.168.10.0/24 after its Gi0/0 return route is withdrawn.
No filtering.

prompt: After the primary link fails, PC-A's request reaches PC-B over the backup. What does the evidence show?
options: Different ADs in the two directions prevent replies from being forwarded
R1 must use a /32 instead of a /24 before PC-B can reply
R1’s outbound /24 is enough to establish R2’s route back to PC-A
R2 needs its own route to PC-A, and no such route remains installed
explanation: R1's backup delivers the request, but R2's only return route used the failed primary. R2 needs its own route back to PC-A.

whyWrong.0: AD is local, and the two directions need no matching values.
whyWrong.1: The /24 already delivered the request.
whyWrong.2: Each router has its own routing table.

exhibit.title: Equal-preference paths violate the standby policy
exhibit.text:
ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 Gi0/0 10.0.12.2
ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 Gi0/1 10.0.13.2
Both transits work. The installed /24 shows two static next hops at [1/0].

prompt: Policy wants Gi0/0 as primary and Gi0/1 as standby, but both routes have AD 1. What is the fix?
options: Remove both routes and change the LAN mask to /25
Raise the Gi0/1 candidate’s distance above 1 for the same /24
Give Gi0/1 a more-specific /25 so it becomes less preferred
Increase the Gi0/0 route’s distance above the Gi0/1 route
explanation: Both routes have the default AD 1 and so share traffic. Raise the Gi0/1 route's AD above 1 for the same /24.

whyWrong.0: No addressing fault is shown.
whyWrong.2: A longer prefix would attract traffic despite higher AD.
whyWrong.3: That would make Gi0/1 the preferred route.

exhibit.title: Construct matching primary and standby routes
exhibit.text:
Destination LAN: 198.51.100.64/26
Required primary: R1 Gi0/0 to directly adjacent 10.0.12.2
Required standby: R1 Gi0/1 to directly adjacent 10.0.13.2, AD 150
Both peers and the complete return path work. No other candidate for this /26 exists.

prompt: Which two configured routes meet the policy, with Gi0/0 primary and Gi0/1 backup for 198.51.100.64/26? (Choose two.)
explanation: Both routes must describe the same /26. The primary uses the default AD 1 and the backup uses AD 150.

whyWrong.1: That is a /27, a different prefix that can attract traffic.
whyWrong.2: AD 255 is never installed.
whyWrong.3: AD 200 on the primary route would make the backup preferred.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
Complete relevant R1 routes:
C 192.168.10.0/24, Gi0/2
C 10.0.12.0/30, Gi0/0
S 192.168.20.0/24 [1/0] via 10.0.12.2
Complete relevant R2 routes (no default):
C 10.0.12.0/30, Gi0/0
C 192.168.20.0/24, Gi0/2

prompt: Interfaces and PC gateways are correct and nothing is filtered. PC-A (192.168.10.11) pings PC-B (192.168.20.12). What happens?
options: The request fails because R1 needs a /32 for every PC.
The request can reach PC-B, but R2 lacks a route for its reply to PC-A.
R2 learns the return route automatically from the received request.
Both directions work because the transit network is connected.
explanation: R1 has the outbound /24, so the request arrives. R2 has no route to PC-A's LAN, so the reply is lost.

whyWrong.0: The /24 already covers PC-B.
whyWrong.2: A received packet does not install a return route.
whyWrong.3: The reply goes to PC-A's LAN, not the transit subnet.

exhibit.title: Two transits share one destination-facing interface
exhibit.text:
R1 has /24 primary via R2 on Gi0/0 AD 1 and same-prefix backup via R2 on Gi0/1 AD 5.
Both transits stay up and the peer addresses remain reachable.
R2’s only interface into that destination LAN becomes administratively down.
No tracking or alternate route into that LAN exists.

prompt: R2's LAN interface fails. Which two conclusions follow? (Choose two.)
options: R1 must withdraw the primary because the final LAN is unavailable
Changing the backup AD alone repairs R2’s failed LAN
R1’s default automatically replaces its still-installed /24
R1 can retain its installed primary even though delivery now fails
R1’s backup through the same R2 does not bypass the failed LAN
explanation: With no tracking, R1 keeps its primary while the local transit is up. The backup also leads to R2, so neither avoids the failed LAN.

whyWrong.0: R1 only checks its local interface and next hop.
whyWrong.1: AD changes cannot repair R2's LAN.
whyWrong.2: A default does not replace a still-installed /24.

exhibit.title: Alternate recursive next-hop resolution
exhibit.text:
R1 configuration:
ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.12.2
ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 Gi0/1 10.0.13.2 5
Independent installed resolver after Gi0/0 failure:
S 10.0.12.2/32 [1/0] via 10.0.13.2, Gi0/1
The Gi0/1 peer is reachable and can reach 10.0.12.2.

prompt: After Gi0/0 fails, R1 still shows the remote /24 at distance 1 instead of the distance-5 route. Why?
options: The primary is automatically converted into a fully specified route.
The next-hop-only primary can resolve through the surviving host route
Both static candidates must be installed whenever their prefixes match.
The backup /24 is more specific than the primary /24.
explanation: The primary is next-hop-only, so it resolves its next hop recursively. The surviving /32 route keeps that next hop reachable through Gi0/1, so the AD-1 route stays installed.

whyWrong.0: The route stays next-hop-only and is not converted.
whyWrong.2: Only the preferred AD-1 route installs for the same prefix.
whyWrong.3: Both candidates are the same /24.

exhibit.title: Different ping results with incomplete evidence
exhibit.text:
R1’s ordinary ping to PC-B succeeds.
PC-A behind R1 cannot ping PC-B.
The engineer has not yet recorded R1’s ping source, PC-A’s gateway, or R2’s return routes.
No further fault evidence is supplied.

prompt: A test works from one source and fails from another. What do you do before changing routing?
options: Compare the two test sources, host configuration and actual return routes
Raise all static distances to force a new path
Change PC-A’s mask so it includes the remote destination
Assume R2 lacks a return route and add a default immediately
explanation: The evidence does not identify the cause. Compare the two sources, their host settings and the return routes first.

whyWrong.1: No AD fault has been shown.
whyWrong.2: Widening the mask breaks the addressing design.
whyWrong.3: A missing return route is possible but not proven.

prompt: What is the default administrative distance of a static route?
explanation: A static route has AD 1 unless you add a different distance at the end of the command.

whyWrong.0: AD 0 is a connected route.
whyWrong.2: 5 is not a default value.
whyWrong.3: 110 is OSPF.

prompt: Which mask makes a static route a host route?
explanation: A host route uses mask 255.255.255.255 (/32) and matches one address.

whyWrong.0: That is a /24 network route.
whyWrong.1: That is a /31 point-to-point network.
whyWrong.3: That mask belongs to the default route.

prompt: How do you turn a static route into a floating static backup?
options: Use a /32 mask on the same destination
Add a higher distance to the same prefix
Use a longer prefix than the primary uses
Point it at a different type of interface
explanation: A floating static has the same prefix as the preferred route and a higher administrative distance at the end of the line.

whyWrong.0: A /32 is a different, more specific prefix.
whyWrong.2: A longer prefix wins longest match instead of waiting.
whyWrong.3: The interface type does not set preference.

prompt: What happens to a route with administrative distance 255?
options: It is the most preferred route
It is installed only when no other route exists
It is never installed in the routing table
It becomes the default route
explanation: A route with distance 255 is never installed.

whyWrong.0: The lowest AD is the most preferred.
whyWrong.1: AD 255 is not installed even as a last resort.
whyWrong.3: A default route is 0.0.0.0/0, whatever its distance.
